Dimension of polynomial growth harmonic functions on locally conformally flat manifolds with nonnegative Ricci curvature

Xiaohan Cai Address: School of Mathematical Sciences, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai 200240, China Email address: xiaohancai@sjtu.edu.cn and Mijia Lai Address: School of Mathematical Sciences, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai 200240, China Email address: laimijia@sjtu.edu.cn
Abstract.

Let ℋd​(M)\mathcal{H}_{d}(M) denote the space of harmonic functions with polynomial growth of degree at most dd on a complete Riemannian manifold (M,g)(M,g). Yau raised two fundamental questions regarding ℋd​(M)\mathcal{H}_{d}(M) on complete manifolds with nonnegative Ricci curvature. The first question is the finite dimensionality of ℋd​(M)\mathcal{H}_{d}(M), which was confirmed by Colding and Minicozzi. The second question asks whether a sharp upper bound given by its Euclidean analog dim⁡ℋd​(ℝn)\operatorname{dim}\mathcal{H}_{d}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) holds. We verify that the second question is true on locally conformally flat manifolds. Indeed, one can precisely determine the value of dimℋd​(M)\dim\mathcal{H}_{d}(M) case by case.

1. Introduction

The study of harmonic functions on complete noncompact Riemannian manifolds with nonnegative Ricci curvature is a central topic connecting geometric analysis, potential theory, and the large-scale geometry of manifolds. The subject originated with Yau’s classical Liouville theorem [32], which establishes that every positive harmonic function must be constant on a complete manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature. The local gradient estimates of Cheng and Yau [6] subsequently provided a fundamental analytic tool, producing Harnack inequalities and quantitative control of positive harmonic functions under lower Ricci curvature bounds. Li and Tam [20, 23] developed a complementary potential-theoretic approach that relates spaces of bounded and positive harmonic functions to the number and geometry of the ends of a manifold.

Yau’s seminal result also opened an interesting direction of research : the study of the space of harmonic functions with at most polynomial growth. For every fixed d>0d>0, let

ℋd(M):={u:Δu=0,|u(x)|≤C(1+r(x))d}\mathcal{H}_{d}(M):=\{u:\Delta u=0,\ |u(x)|\leq C(1+r(x))^{d}\}

denote the space of harmonic functions of polynomial growth of at most degree dd. Yau raised two fundamental questions regarding ℋd​(M)\mathcal{H}_{d}(M) when MM has nonnegative Ricci curvature:

  1. Q1

    finite dimensionality: is it true that dimℋd​(M)<∞\dim\mathcal{H}_{d}(M)<\infty?

  2. Q2

    sharp Euclidean comparison: is it true that dimℋd​(Mn)≤dimℋd​(ℝn)\dim\mathcal{H}_{d}(M^{n})\leq\dim\mathcal{H}_{d}(\mathbb{R}^{n})?

For brevity, write hd​(M)=dimℋd​(M)h_{d}(M)=\dim\mathcal{H}_{d}(M). It is a classical result that any harmonic function with polynomial growth on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} must be a harmonic polynomial. For any fixed integer d≥1d\geq 1, it is a fun exercise to show that

hd​(ℝn)=(n+d−1n−1)+(n+d−2n−1).h_{d}(\mathbb{R}^{n})=\binom{n+d-1}{n-1}+\binom{n+d-2}{n-1}.

Regarding Q1, Li–Tam [22] first established this for surfaces with finite total curvature. Colding and Minicozzi [8] verified the finite dimensionality of ℋd​(M)\mathcal{H}_{d}(M) in general dimension. Li [17] also gave an independent proof. Later, Colding and Minicozzi [9] proved a Weyl type bound

hd​(Mn)≤C⁡(n)​dn−1+o⁡(dn−1),h_{d}(M^{n})\leq C(n)d^{n-1}+o(d^{n-1}),

which is asymptotically sharp in the power of dd since hd​(ℝn)∼2(n−1)!​dn−1h_{d}(\mathbb{R}^{n})\sim\frac{2}{(n-1)!}d^{n-1} as d→∞d\to\infty.

For Q2, the case d=1d=1 is known by  [21]. One also has rigidity in view of  [7]. More precisely, let MnM^{n} be a complete noncompact manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature, and suppose that h1​(Mn)=h1​(ℝn)=n+1h_{1}(M^{n})=h_{1}(\mathbb{R}^{n})=n+1, then MM must be isometric to ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}.

However, for d>1d>1, the Euclidean comparison in general is false. Donnelly [10] constructed, in every dimension n≥5n\geq 5, a complete noncompact manifold with Ric≥0\operatorname{Ric}\geq 0 carrying more than n+1n+1 linearly independent harmonic functions of subquadratic growth. Hence, for a suitable 1<d<21<d<2, Donnelly’s example shows

hd​(Mn)>hd​(ℝn)=n+1.h_{d}(M^{n})>h_{d}(\mathbb{R}^{n})=n+1.

Nevertheless, the integer-degree Euclidean comparison remains an open question. Under the assumption of maximal volume growth and uniqueness of the tangent cone at infinity, Huang [11, 12] established the Euclidean comparison asymptotically with a sharp coefficient, i.e.,

limd→∞hd​(Mn)dn−1=2​β(n−1)!,\lim_{d\to\infty}\frac{h_{d}(M^{n})}{d^{n-1}}=\frac{2\beta}{(n-1)!},

where β\beta is the asymptotic volume ratio of MM. Li–Wang [24] proved a similar result when MM has nonnegative sectional curvature. Indeed, the Euclidean comparison is still an open question on non-negatively curved manifolds. There is a recent breakthrough by Lin-Wang-Xu [26], in which they showed that on a three-dimensional manifold with nonnegative sectional curvature and β>0\beta>0, for any integer d≥0d\geq 0, hd​(M3)≤hd​(ℝ3)h_{d}(M^{3})\leq h_{d}(\mathbb{R}^{3}). Moreover, if the equality holds for some d≥1d\geq 1, then M3M^{3} is isometric to ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}.

In this paper, we give an affirmative answer to Q2 on locally conformally flat manifolds:

Theorem A.

Let (Mn,g)​(n≥3)(M^{n},g)(n\geq 3) be a complete noncompact locally conformally flat manifolds with nonnegative Ricci curvature, then for each d≥0d\geq 0,

hd​(Mn)≤hd​(ℝn).h_{d}(M^{n})\leq h_{d}(\mathbb{R}^{n}).

Moreover, if the equality holds for some integer d≥1d\geq 1, then MM is isometric to ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}.

Let (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) be a complete noncompact manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature. Denote by β\beta the asymptotic volume ratio of (M,g)(M,g), i.e.,

β=limr→∞vol⁡(B⁡(p,r))ωn​rn.\beta=\lim_{r\to\infty}\frac{\operatorname{vol}(B(p,r))}{\omega_{n}r^{n}}.

The above limit is independent of the choice of the base point p∈Mp\in M. When β>0\beta>0, MM is said to have Euclidean volume growth.

Locally conformally flat manifolds with nonnegative Ricci curvature have been completely classified by Zhu [33] and Carron–Herzlich [4]. According to this classification, one essential case to study is when (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) takes the form (ℝn,g=e2​w​g0)(\mathbb{R}^{n},g=e^{2w}g_{0}), for which Ma and Qing [29] developed a fundamental theory on the asymptotic exponent of the conformal factor ww.

We now explain in some details of Ma-Qing’s theory. There exists m∈[0,1]m\in[0,1] such that

lim infx→∞w⁡(x)ln⁡|x|=−m.\liminf_{x\to\infty}\frac{w(x)}{\ln|x|}=-m.

Moreover, there exists an exceptional set EE, which is nn-thin at infinity (in the sense of nn-potential theory) such that

limx→∞,x∉Ew⁡(x)ln⁡|x|=−m.\lim_{x\to\infty,x\notin E}\frac{w(x)}{\ln|x|}=-m.

In a recent breakthrough [28], Ma refined the above estimate to the following: setting w¯​(r)=inf|x|=rw⁡(x)\underline{w}(r)=\inf_{|x|=r}w(x), there exists a strong ℰ\mathcal{E}-set EE, such that

(1.1) w(x)=w¯(|x|)+o(1),x→∞andx∉E.w(x)=\underline{w}(|x|)+o(1),\quad x\to\infty\quad\text{and}\quad x\notin E.

Using this refined radial symmetry of ww, Ma [28] showed that

(1.2) β1n−1=1−m.\beta^{\frac{1}{n-1}}=1-m.

Furthermore, Ma computed the exact values of the scale-invariant integral of scalar curvature, limr→∞1rn−2​∫BrRg​⁡d​Vg\lim_{r\to\infty}\frac{1}{r^{n-2}}\int_{B_{r}}R_{g}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}V_{g}, which affirmatively answers a question of Yau on the finiteness of scalar curvature for complete manifolds with nonnegative Ricci curvature in the locally conformally flat setting.

Building on this asymptotic analysis of the conformal factor, we establish our main result by treating the two cases β=0\beta=0 and β>0\beta>0 separately.

Theorem B.

Let g=e2​w​g0g=e^{2w}g_{0} be a smooth and complete metric on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} with nonnegative Ricci curvature, suppose β=0\beta=0, then for every finite d≥0d\geq 0,

ℋd​(ℝn,g)=ℝ.\mathcal{H}_{d}(\mathbb{R}^{n},g)=\mathbb{R}.

For β>0\beta>0, in view of (1.2), we have m<1m<1. Set a=1−m∈(0,1]a=1-m\in(0,1] and define

𝒞a=([0,∞)×𝕊n−1,d​ρ2+a2​ρ2​g𝕊n−1).\mathcal{C}_{a}=\bigl([0,\infty)\times\mathbb{S}^{n-1},d\rho^{2}+a^{2}\rho^{2}g_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}\bigr).
Theorem C.

Let g=e2​w​g0g=e^{2w}g_{0} be a smooth and complete metric on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} with nonnegative Ricci curvature, suppose β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1) , then for every integer d≥1d\geq 1,

dimℋd​(ℝn,g)=dimℋd​(𝒞a)≤dimℋd−1​(ℝn,g0)<dimℋd​(ℝn,g0).\dim\mathcal{H}_{d}(\mathbb{R}^{n},g)=\dim\mathcal{H}_{d}(\mathcal{C}_{a})\leq\dim\mathcal{H}_{d-1}(\mathbb{R}^{n},g_{0})<\dim\mathcal{H}_{d}(\mathbb{R}^{n},g_{0}).

In spirit, the study in this paper can be regarded as an extension of the Li–Tam’s result [22] to higher dimension. As a precursor for the main result, we first need to establish a comparison between the distance induced by the conformal metric g=e2​w​g0g=e^{2w}g_{0} and the underlying Euclidean distance.

Theorem 1.1.

Let g=e2​w​g0g=e^{2w}g_{0} be a conformal metric on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} with nonnegative Ricci curvature and β>0\beta>0. Let r⁡(x)r(x) denote the distance function to the origin induced by gg, then

(1.3) limx→∞ln⁡r⁡(x)ln⁡|x|=1−m.\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{\ln r(x)}{\ln|x|}=1-m.

The proof of Theorem 1.1 relies on Ma-Qing’s theory. With new advances by Ma, the relation (1.3) even holds when β=0\beta=0 and can be implicitly deduced from Ma’s argument.

Distance comparison enables us to translate geometric and function-theoretic information into Euclidean terms. Then the asymptotic analysis 1.1 helps to establish a bijection, through a blow-down procedure, between ℋd​(ℝn,g)\mathcal{H}_{d}(\mathbb{R}^{n},g) and ℋd​(𝒞a)\mathcal{H}_{d}(\mathcal{C}_{a}). The difficulty arises from the presence of a strong ℰ\mathcal{E}-set EE in 1.1 and the lack of uniform ellipticity for the limiting harmonic equations, which prevent convergence in the standard GG-convergence framework [34]. To circumvent this, we devise a weighted GG-convergence scheme and then carry through the blow-down argument and the dimension estimates.

The organization of the paper is as follows. In Section 2, we prove Theorem B. In Section 3, we provide a proof for Theorem 1.1 even though this result is now subsumed by  [28]. The proof does not need to appeal to Ma’s new theory and has its own independent interest. In Section 4, we discuss the blow-down scheme and weighted GG-convergence. In Section 5, we prove Theorem C. In the last section, dealing with remaining cases, we conclude the proof of Theorem A.

Declaration on the use of AI: The authors obtained Theorem 1.1 and then developed the overall strategy for the proofs of Theorem C — the main body of Theorem A — prior to any involvement of AI in the proofs. AI was subsequently used to assist in generating certain technical details. All arguments were written by the authors. We take full responsibility for the content of this manuscript.

2. The case with vanishing asymptotic volume ratio

Kasue and Carron proved Liouville theorems under sublinear diameter growth of geodesic spheres [14, 15, 3]. Carron’s formulation [3, Theorem 1.1] is particularly convenient here.

Proposition 2.1.

Let (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) be complete with Ricg≥0\operatorname{Ric}_{g}\geq 0. Assume that, for some p∈Mp\in M,

diamg⁡(∂BRg​(p))=o⁡(R).\operatorname{diam}_{g}\bigl(\partial B_{R}^{g}(p)\bigr)=o(R).

Then every harmonic function of polynomial growth of finite degree in MM must be constant.

Proof of Theorem B.

Adopting the notation in [28], i.e., set w¯​(r)=inf|x|=rw⁡(x)\underline{w}(r)=\inf_{|x|=r}w(x), in view of the assumption that β=0\beta=0, it follows that limr→∞w¯​(r)ln⁡r=−1\lim_{r\to\infty}\frac{\underline{w}(r)}{\ln r}=-1. Consider the radial metric g¯=e2​w¯​g0\underline{g}=e^{2\underline{w}}g_{0}. Introducing the intrinsic radial coordinates ρ⁡(r)=∫0rew¯​(s)​⁡𝑑s\rho(r)=\int_{0}^{r}e^{\underline{w}(s)}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}s and the warping function a⁡(ρ)=r​ew¯​(r),a(\rho)=re^{\underline{w}(r)}, we find

g¯=d​ρ2+a​(ρ)2​g𝕊n−1.\underline{g}=d\rho^{2}+a(\rho)^{2}g_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}.

Based on the asymptotic radial symmetry (1.1), Ma [28, Page 29] showed that

(2.1) BRg¯⊂BRg⊂BR+o⁡(R)g¯,B^{\underline{g}}_{R}\subset B^{g}_{R}\subset B^{\underline{g}}_{R+o(R)},

Combining this with the volume growth assumption β=0\beta=0 and w≥w¯w\geq\underline{w}, we get

0=limR→+∞v​o​lg​(Bg​(p,R))|𝔹n|​Rn\displaystyle 0=\lim_{R\to+\infty}\frac{vol_{g}(B^{g}(p,R))}{|\mathbb{B}^{n}|R^{n}} ≥limR→+∞v​o​lg¯​(Bg¯​(p,R))|𝔹n|​Rn\displaystyle\geq\lim_{R\to+\infty}\frac{vol_{\underline{g}}(B^{\underline{g}}(p,R))}{|\mathbb{B}^{n}|R^{n}}
=limR→+∞a​r​e​ag¯​(∂Bg¯​(p,R))|𝕊n−1|​Rn−1=limρ→+∞an−1​(ρ)ρn−1\displaystyle=\lim_{R\to+\infty}\frac{area_{\underline{g}}(\partial B^{\underline{g}}(p,R))}{|\mathbb{S}^{n-1}|R^{n-1}}=\lim_{\rho\to+\infty}\frac{a^{n-1}(\rho)}{\rho^{n-1}}

It follows that

(2.2) a′​(ρ)→0,a⁡(ρ)ρ→0,as ​ρ→+∞.a^{\prime}(\rho)\to 0,\qquad\frac{a(\rho)}{\rho}\to 0,\qquad\text{as }\rho\to+\infty.

Therefore,

diam⁡(∂BRg¯)≤π​a​(R)=o⁡(R).\operatorname{diam}(\partial B^{\underline{g}}_{R})\leq\pi a(R)=o(R).

By 2.1, one easily see that diam⁡(∂BRg)=o⁡(R)\operatorname{diam}(\partial B^{g}_{R})=o(R) as well. Hence the conclusion follows from Proposition 2.1. ∎

We also include a simple ODE argument for radially symmetric conformal metric (ℝn,g=e2​w​(|x|)​g0)(\mathbb{R}^{n},g=e^{2w(|x|)}g_{0}) with nonnegative Ricci curvature and β=0\beta=0.

Theorem 2.2.

Let

g=e2​w​(|x|)​g0g=e^{2w(|x|)}g_{0}

be a complete and smooth rotationally symmetric metric on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} with nonnegative Ricci curvature. Assume β=0\beta=0, then for every d≥0d\geq 0

ℋd​(ℝn,g)=ℝ.\mathcal{H}_{d}(\mathbb{R}^{n},g)=\mathbb{R}.
Proof.

As above, we can now assume g=d​ρ2+a​(ρ)2​g𝕊n−1g=d\rho^{2}+a(\rho)^{2}g_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}} under the intrinsic radial coordinates and a⁡(ρ)a(\rho) satisfies (2.2).

u⁡(ρ,θ)=∑ℓ=0∞∑mvℓ,m​(ρ)​Yℓ,m​(θ),u(\rho,\theta)=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}\sum_{m}v_{\ell,m}(\rho)Y_{\ell,m}(\theta),

prevents a positive regular solution from acquiring a first zero or a first nonpositive derivative.

q⁡(s)≥c∀s≥S.q(s)\geq c\qquad\forall s\geq S.

3. Distance comparison for Euclidean volume growth

We carry out the proof of Theorem C in the following three sections. The general strategy is inspired by Lin’s work on asymptotically conic elliptic operators [25]. In this section, we compare the intrinsic distance of the conformal metric with the Euclidean distance, thereby translating intrinsic polynomial growth into growth estimates adapted to Euclidean rescaling. In Section 4, we establish a weighted compactness theorem for the rescaled harmonic equations and show that normalized blow-down sequences converge to harmonic functions on a fixed metric cone. In Section 5, we exploit the spectral decomposition on the limiting cone to obtain a uniform L2L^{2} growth ratio upper bound. A scale-dependent Gram-Schmidt procedure then allows us to blow down a finite-dimensional space of harmonic functions simultaneously while preserving linear independence, leading to the desired dimension estimate.

In this section, we shall prove Theorem 1.1. Two fundamental constants that we frequently refer to are:

  • •

    β\beta: the asymptotic volume ratio of a complete noncompact manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature, i.e.,

    β=limr→∞vol⁡(B⁡(p,r))ωn​rn.\beta=\lim_{r\to\infty}\frac{\operatorname{vol}(B(p,r))}{\omega_{n}r^{n}}.
  • •

    mm: the asymptotic exponent of the conformal factor. Let (ℝn,e2​w​g0),(n≥3)(\mathbb{R}^{n},e^{2w}g_{0}),(n\geq 3) be a complete Riemannian manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature, then there exists m∈[0,1]m\in[0,1] (see  [29, Theorem 1.3]), such that

    (3.1) lim infx→∞w⁡(x)ln⁡|x|=−m.\liminf_{x\to\infty}\frac{w(x)}{\ln|x|}=-m.

We shall first derive a technical tool: a refined Harnack inequality Proposition 3.2. Then we divide the proof into two steps, following the strategy of Li-Tam [22]. The first step appeals to the pointwise lower bound of the conformal factor ww due to Ma-Qing, and a lower bound of the gg-volume of the Euclidean ball is obtained. Then an elementary inclusion relation between the geodesic ball and the Euclidean ball implies that

lim infx→∞ln⁡r⁡(x)ln⁡|x|≥1−m.\liminf_{x\to\infty}\frac{\ln r(x)}{\ln|x|}\geq 1-m.

The refined Harnack inequality is used in this part.

The difficulty of the second step lies in the fact that there is no pointwise upper bound of the conformal factor ww. In contrast, inspired by [29, Theorem 3.1, Proposition 4.1], an upper bound of the gg-volume of the Euclidean ball could be derived via several involved results in nonlinear potential theory. It follows analogously that

lim supx→∞ln⁡r⁡(x)ln⁡|x|≤1−m.\limsup_{x\to\infty}\frac{\ln r(x)}{\ln|x|}\leq 1-m.

Once again, the refined Harnack inequality Proposition 3.2 is used in this step.

We also include a proof relating the the comparison of two distance functions to the asymptotic volume ratio β\beta. The conformal invariance of the nn-Laplace operator indicates that ln⁡|x|\ln|x| is the nn-Green function on (Mn,g)(M^{n},g). Meanwhile, ∫1r⁡(x)A​(t)−1n−1​⁡𝑑t\int_{1}^{r(x)}A(t)^{-\frac{1}{n-1}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t is the nn-Green function when (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) is radially symmetric. Combining with the refined Harnack inequality, a comparison principle argument is applied to these functions to show that

lim supx→∞ln⁡r⁡(x)ln⁡|x|≤β1n−1.\limsup_{x\to\infty}\frac{\ln r(x)}{\ln|x|}\leq\beta^{\frac{1}{n-1}}.
Remark 3.1.

In view of 2.1, the conclusion of Theorem 1.1 follows. Moreover it also holds when β=0\beta=0. We present our proof anyway as it has independent interest.

3.1. A refined Harnack inequality


In this subsection, we prove a refined Harnack inequality which serves as a basis analytical tool in each step.

Proposition 3.2.

Let (ℝn,e2​w​g0)(\mathbb{R}^{n},e^{2w}g_{0}) be a complete Riemannian manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature and β>0\beta>0. Then

s⁡(R)≤i⁡(R)​eo⁡(1)as ​R→+∞,s(R)\leq i(R)e^{o(1)}\quad\text{as }R\to+\infty,

where s⁡(r):=sup∂Bg​(0,r)ln⁡|x|s(r):=\sup_{\partial B^{g}(0,r)}\ln|x| and i⁡(r):=inf∂Bg​(0,r)ln⁡|x|i(r):=\inf_{\partial B^{g}(0,r)}\ln|x|.

We first establish several simple lemmas.

Lemma 3.3.

Let (ℝn,e2​w​g0)(\mathbb{R}^{n},e^{2w}g_{0}) be a complete Riemannian manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature. Denote r⁡(x):=distg⁡(x,0)r(x):=\operatorname{dist}_{g}(x,0) the distance to the origin. Then

−Δn​ln⁡r⁡(x)≥0.-\Delta_{n}\ln r(x)\geq 0.
Proof.

The proof is by a direct calculation.

Recall that the Harnack inequality for a nonnegative nn-harmonic function uu on B⁡(0,R)⊂ℝnB(0,R)\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} states as: there exists a constant C⁡(n)C(n) such that

3.3. Upper bound by mm

Proposition 3.8.

Let (ℝn,e2​w​g0),(n≥3)(\mathbb{R}^{n},e^{2w}g_{0}),(n\geq 3) be a complete Riemannian manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature and β>0\beta>0. Then

lim supx→∞ln⁡r⁡(x)ln⁡|x|≤1−m.\limsup_{x\to\infty}\frac{\ln r(x)}{\ln|x|}\leq 1-m.

Since there is no pointwise upper bound of the conformal factor ww like the lower bound 3.5, the argument in Proposition 3.7 could not be applied directly to prove Proposition 3.8. Instead, inspired by Ma-Qing’s work on the asymptotic upper bound of ww out of some exceptional set (see [29, Theorem 3.1]), we shall utilize several deep results in nonlinear potential theory to derive an upper bound of the gg-volume of Euclidean balls.

We start with the main technical lemma, whose main part is a modification of [29, proposition 4.1].

(3.6) −Δn​w0=Ricg​(∇gw0|∇gw0|g,∇gw0|∇gw0|g)​|∇w0|n−2​e2​w0=:fon ​ℝn∖{0}.-\Delta_{n}w_{0}=\mathrm{Ric}_{g}\left(\frac{\nabla^{g}w_{0}}{|\nabla^{g}w_{0}|_{g}},\frac{\nabla^{g}w_{0}}{|\nabla^{g}w_{0}|_{g}}\right)|\nabla w_{0}|^{n-2}e^{2w_{0}}=:f\quad\text{on }\mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus\{0\}.

In this subsection, we also include a result showing that the ratio of two distances is bounded from above by the asymptotic volume ratio β\beta. This is similar to that of [22, Theorem 2.5].

4. Weighted GG-convergence

In this section we prove the convergence statement (Theorem 4.2) needed in the subsequent blow-down argument . The terminology “weighted GG-convergence” is used only to emphasize the analogy with the classical GG-compactness theorem for uniformly elliptic divergence-form operators (see, for example, [34, Theorem 3]).

Let g=e2​w​g0g=e^{2w}g_{0} be a complete conformal metric on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, n≥3n\geq 3, with Ricg≥0\operatorname{Ric}_{g}\geq 0 and β>0\beta>0. We write

w¯​(R):=inf|x|=Rw⁡(x).\underline{w}(R):=\inf_{|x|=R}w(x).

Let m∈(0,1)m\in(0,1) be the asymptotic exponent of ww (see 3.1), and set a:=1−m.a:=1-m.

Let hh be a gg-harmonic function, then the conformal transformation formula gives

Δgh=0⟺div(e(n−2)​w∇h)=0,\Delta_{g}h=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{div}\bigl(e^{(n-2)w}\nabla h\bigr)=0,

where div,∇\operatorname{div},\nabla are the divergence and the gradient in the standard Euclidean space respectively.

In view of the asymptotic exponent of the conformal factor 1.1, one may expect that a tangent cone at infinity of (ℝn,g)(\mathbb{R}^{n},g) is the metric cone (ℝn,|x|−2​m​g0)(\mathbb{R}^{n},|x|^{-2m}g_{0}). It is probably difficult to fully establish this geometric statement due to the presence of that strong ℰ\mathcal{E}-set in 1.1. Nevertheless, one can blow down a gg-harmonic function to a harmonic function on the limit cone, as we now explain.

For R>0R>0, define

(4.1) PR​(y):=exp⁡((n−2)​(w⁡(R​y)−w¯​(R))),QR​(y):=exp⁡(n⁡(w⁡(R​y)−w¯​(R))).P_{R}(y):=\exp\bigl((n-2)(w(Ry)-\underline{w}(R))\bigr),\qquad Q_{R}(y):=\exp\bigl(n(w(Ry)-\underline{w}(R))\bigr).

The limiting weights are

P∞​(y):=|y|−m⁡(n−2),Q∞​(y):=|y|−m​n.P_{\infty}(y):=|y|^{-m(n-2)},\qquad Q_{\infty}(y):=|y|^{-mn}.

Set uR​(y):=cR−1​h​(R​y),(cR≠0)u_{R}(y):=c_{R}^{-1}h(Ry),(c_{R}\neq 0), then it solves

div(PR∇uR)=0.\operatorname{div}(P_{R}\nabla u_{R})=0.

We shall prove that a proper blow down limit of a gg-harmonic function hh converges to a solution of the limiting equation

(4.2) L∞u:=div(P∞∇u)=div(|y|−m⁡(n−2)∇u),L_{\infty}u:=\operatorname{div}(P_{\infty}\nabla u)=\operatorname{div}\bigl(|y|^{-m(n-2)}\nabla u\bigr),

which is exactly the Laplace–Beltrami operator of the limiting cone

(4.3) 𝒞a=([0,∞)×𝕊n−1,d​ρ2+a2​ρ2​g𝕊n−1),ρ=1a​|y|a.\mathcal{C}_{a}=\bigl([0,\infty)\times\mathbb{S}^{n-1},d\rho^{2}+a^{2}\rho^{2}g_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}\bigr),\qquad\rho=\frac{1}{a}|y|^{a}.

More explicitly, we start with a convergence result for the operators div(PR∇⋅)\operatorname{div}(P_{R}\nabla\cdot). Ideally, one would hope for the sequence of operators div(PR∇⋅)\operatorname{div}(P_{R}\nabla\cdot) to converge to the limiting operator div(P∞∇⋅)\operatorname{div}(P_{\infty}\nabla\cdot) in the well-studied GG-convergence framework, since then Theorem C would follow directly from [25, Theorem 2.13]. However, the presence of the strong ℰ\mathcal{E}-set in the asymptotic behavior of ww and the lack of boundedness of the limiting weight P∞P_{\infty} make such GG-convergence unattainable. To overcome this obstacle, we instead show that the operators are III\operatorname{III}-convergent in the sense of [34, Page 76]. Building on this, we then establish a matched compactness result for solutions, which plays a vital role in subsequent blow-down arguments.

First, we isolate several precise consequences of the asymptotic analysis of the conformal factor ww, resulting the III\operatorname{III}-convergence of the operators div(PR∇⋅)\operatorname{div}(P_{R}\nabla\cdot) (i.e. 4.4). The proof utilizes the convergence of r​w¯′​(r)r\underline{w}^{\prime}(r), the spherical exponential-average estimate, and the annular gg-volume estimate established in [28].

Proposition 4.1.

For every Λ>0\Lambda>0, as R→∞R\to\infty,

(4.4) PR→P∞in ​L1​(BΛ),P_{R}\to P_{\infty}\quad\text{in }L^{1}(B_{\Lambda}),
(4.5) QR→Q∞in ​L1​(BΛ).Q_{R}\to Q_{\infty}\quad\text{in }L^{1}(B_{\Lambda}).

In particular,

supR≥RΛ∫BΛPR​⁡𝑑y<∞,supR≥RΛ∫BΛQR​⁡𝑑y<∞.\sup_{R\geq R_{\Lambda}}\int_{B_{\Lambda}}P_{R}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y<\infty,\qquad\sup_{R\geq R_{\Lambda}}\int_{B_{\Lambda}}Q_{R}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y<\infty.

Moreover, there exists cΛ>0c_{\Lambda}>0 and RΛ>0R_{\Lambda}>0 such that

(4.6) ew​(R​y)−w¯​(R)≥cΛfor all ​y∈BΛ,R≥RΛ.e^{w(Ry)-\underline{w}(R)}\geq c_{\Lambda}\qquad\text{for all }y\in B_{\Lambda},\quad R\geq R_{\Lambda}.
Proof.

The radial analysis in [28, Lemma 2.6] gives

(4.7) r​w¯′​(r)→−mas ​r→+∞.r\underline{w}^{\prime}(r)\to-m\qquad\text{as }r\to+\infty.

Hence, for every 0<δ<Λ<∞0<\delta<\Lambda<\infty,

w¯​(R​s)−w¯​(R)→−m​log⁡s,as ​R→+∞,\underline{w}(Rs)-\underline{w}(R)\to-m\log s,\qquad\text{as }R\to+\infty,

uniformly for s∈[δ,Λ]s\in[\delta,\Lambda]. Therefore, for q=n−2q=n-2 and q=nq=n,

(4.8) exp⁡(q⁡(w¯​(R​|y|)−w¯​(R)))→|y|−m​q,as ​R→+∞,\exp\bigl(q(\underline{w}(R|y|)-\underline{w}(R))\bigr)\to|y|^{-mq},\qquad\text{as }R\to+\infty,

uniformly on every compact annulus.

On a noncompact region, a direct integration of 4.7 implies the following estimate: for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0, there exists Rϵ>0R_{\epsilon}>0 such that for all R≥RϵR\geq R_{\epsilon} and s≥RϵRs\geq\frac{R_{\epsilon}}{R}, there holds

(4.9) exp⁡(q⁡(w¯​(R​s)−w¯​(R)))≤max⁡{s−q⁡(m−ϵ),s−q⁡(m+ϵ)},q∈{n−2,n}.\exp\bigl(q(\underline{w}(Rs)-\underline{w}(R))\bigr)\leq\max\{s^{-q(m-\epsilon)},s^{-q(m+\epsilon)}\},\qquad q\in\{n-2,n\}.

We first prove the convergence of PRP_{R}. Set

P¯R​(y):=exp⁡((n−2)​(w¯​(R​|y|)−w¯​(R))).\underline{P}_{R}(y):=\exp\bigl((n-2)(\underline{w}(R|y|)-\underline{w}(R))\bigr).

Since w​(x)≥w¯​(|x|)w(x)\geq\underline{w}(|x|), there holds PR≥P¯R.P_{R}\geq\underline{P}_{R}. For a fixed annulus Aδ,ΛA_{\delta,\Lambda}, we have

(4.10) ∫Aδ,Λ(PR−P¯R)​⁡𝑑y=|𝕊n−1|​∫δΛsn−1​exp⁡((n−2)​(w¯​(R​s)−w¯​(R)))​(F⁡(R​s)−1)​⁡𝑑s,\int_{A_{\delta,\Lambda}}(P_{R}-\underline{P}_{R})\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y=|\mathbb{S}^{n-1}|\int_{\delta}^{\Lambda}s^{n-1}\exp\bigl((n-2)(\underline{w}(Rs)-\underline{w}(R))\bigr)\bigl(F(Rs)-1\bigr)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}s,

where

F⁡(t):=1|𝕊n−1|​∫𝕊n−1exp⁡((n−2)​(w⁡(t​θ)−w¯​(t)))​⁡𝑑θ.F(t):=\frac{1}{|\mathbb{S}^{n-1}|}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}\exp\bigl((n-2)(w(t\theta)-\underline{w}(t))\bigr)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\theta.

By the spherical exponential-average estimate in [28, Lemma 4.7], there holds

(4.11) F⁡(t)→1as ​t→+∞.F(t)\to 1\qquad\text{as }t\to+\infty.

It follows from 4.10, 4.8, and 4.11 that

‖PR−P¯R‖L1​(Aδ,Λ)→0as ​R→+∞.\|P_{R}-\underline{P}_{R}\|_{L^{1}(A_{\delta,\Lambda})}\to 0\qquad\text{as }R\to+\infty.

To pass from annuli to the whole ball, we prove uniform integrability near 0. Fix T>1T>1. On the central ball BT/RB_{T/R}, changing variables x=R​yx=Ry yields

∫BT/RPR​(y)​𝑑y=R−n​e−(n−2)​w¯​(R)​∫BTe(n−2)​w​(x)​𝑑x.\int_{B_{T/R}}P_{R}(y)\mathrm{d}y=R^{-n}e^{-(n-2)\underline{w}(R)}\int_{B_{T}}e^{(n-2)w(x)}\mathrm{d}x.

Since w¯​(R)=−m​log⁡R+o⁡(log⁡R)\underline{w}(R)=-m\log R+o(\log R) and n−m⁡(n−2)>0n-m(n-2)>0, the right-hand side tends to zero for each fixed TT. On Bδ\BT/RB_{\delta}\backslash B_{T/R}, decomposing into dyadic annuli and use 4.9 together with 4.10 and 4.11, we obtain

Since the same estimate is immediate for P∞P_{\infty}, combining 4.12 and 4.13 proves 4.4.

We now turn to QRQ_{R}. Define

Q¯R​(y):=exp⁡(n⁡(w¯​(R​|y|)−w¯​(R))).\underline{Q}_{R}(y):=\exp\bigl(n(\underline{w}(R|y|)-\underline{w}(R))\bigr).

Here the numerator is nonnegative because w​(x)≥w¯​(|x|)w(x)\geq\underline{w}(|x|). After the change of variables x=R​yx=Ry, 4.14 implies

‖QR−Q¯R‖L1​(Aδ,Λ)→0\|Q_{R}-\underline{Q}_{R}\|_{L^{1}(A_{\delta,\Lambda})}\to 0

for every fixed annulus. Thus

QR→Q∞in ​L1​(Aδ,Λ).Q_{R}\to Q_{\infty}\quad\text{in }L^{1}(A_{\delta,\Lambda}).

The same central-ball and dyadic-annulus argument as above, now using m​n<nmn<n, 4.9 and 4.14, gives

limδ↓0lim supR→∞∫BδQR​⁡𝑑y=0.\lim_{\delta\downarrow 0}\limsup_{R\to\infty}\int_{B_{\delta}}Q_{R}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y=0.

This proves 4.5.

It remains to prove the lower bound 4.6. We shall verify it in three cases separately. If 0<|y|≤10<|y|\leq 1 and R​|y|R|y| sufficiently large, then w¯\underline{w} is decreasing due to 4.7. Therefore,

w⁡(R​y)−w¯​(R)≥w¯​(R​|y|)−w¯​(R)≥0.w(Ry)-\underline{w}(R)\geq\underline{w}(R|y|)-\underline{w}(R)\geq 0.

If 0<|y|≤10<|y|\leq 1 and R​|y|R|y| remains in a fixed compact interval, then w⁡(R​y)w(Ry) is bounded from below while w¯​(R)→−∞\underline{w}(R)\to-\infty as RR tends to +∞+\infty, so the same expression is bounded from below. If 1≤|y|≤Λ1\leq|y|\leq\Lambda, 4.7 gives

w⁡(R​y)−w¯​(R)≥w¯​(R​|y|)−w¯​(R)≥−(m+1)​log⁡Λw(Ry)-\underline{w}(R)\geq\underline{w}(R|y|)-\underline{w}(R)\geq-(m+1)\log\Lambda

for all sufficiently large RR. This proves 4.6. ∎

In the remaining part of this section, we prove the key convergence theorem for solutions to div(AR∇u)=0\operatorname{div}(A_{R}\nabla u)=0. This can be viewed as an analogue, within the framework of III\operatorname{III}-convergence of operators (as defined in [34, Page 76]), of the classical convergence result for GG-convergent operators (see, for example, [25, (iv) in page 220]).

We denote

d​νR:=QR​(y)​⁡d​y,d​ν∞:=Q∞​(y)​⁡d​y,d\nu_{R}:=Q_{R}(y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y,\qquad d\nu_{\infty}:=Q_{\infty}(y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y,

and, for r>0r>0, define the weighted integral averages

AvR,r⁡(f):=∫Brf​⁡d​νRνR​(Br),Av∞,r⁡(f):=∫Brf​⁡d​ν∞ν∞​(Br).\operatorname{Av}_{R,r}(f):=\frac{\displaystyle\int_{B_{r}}f\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\nu_{R}}{\displaystyle\nu_{R}(B_{r})},\qquad\operatorname{Av}_{\infty,r}(f):=\frac{\displaystyle\int_{B_{r}}f\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\nu_{\infty}}{\displaystyle\nu_{\infty}(B_{r})}.

Then, after passing to a subsequence, there exists a function u∞u_{\infty} satisfying:

    For every 0<Λ′<Λ0<\Lambda^{\prime}<\Lambda,

    uj⇀u∞in ​H1​(BΛ′),anduj→u∞in ​L2​(BΛ′).u_{j}\rightharpoonup u_{\infty}\quad\text{in }H^{1}(B_{\Lambda^{\prime}}),\quad\text{and}\quad u_{j}\to u_{\infty}\quad\text{in }L^{2}(B_{\Lambda^{\prime}}).
  2. (2)

    u∞u_{\infty} is locally bounded near the origin and satisfies

    L∞​u∞=0in ​BΛ.L_{\infty}u_{\infty}=0\qquad\text{in }B_{\Lambda}.

    in the weak sense, where L∞L_{\infty} is defined in 4.2.

  3. (3)

    For every 0<r<Λ0<r<\Lambda,

    (4.17) AvRj,r⁡(uj2)→Av∞,r⁡(u∞2).\operatorname{Av}_{R_{j},r}(u_{j}^{2})\to\operatorname{Av}_{\infty,r}(u_{\infty}^{2}).

    More generally, if u1,j,…,uq,ju_{1,j},\ldots,u_{q,j} are finitely many sequences satisfying the same assumptions and converging simultaneously, then

Proof.

Step 1: Set

≤\displaystyle\leq ∥φ∥L∞(supp∇χϵ)(∫B2​εP∞|∇u∞|2)1/2(∫B2​ϵP∞|∇χε|2)1/2→0.\displaystyle\|\varphi\|_{L^{\infty}(\text{supp}\nabla\chi_{\epsilon})}\left(\int_{B_{2\varepsilon}}P_{\infty}|\nabla u_{\infty}|^{2}\right)^{1/2}\left(\int_{B_{2\epsilon}}P_{\infty}|\nabla\chi_{\varepsilon}|^{2}\right)^{1/2}\to 0.

|uj|+|u∞|≤Mron ​Br.|u_{j}|+|u_{\infty}|\leq M_{r}\qquad\text{on }B_{r}.

5. Simultaneous blow-down

In this section, we combine the distance comparison established in Section 3 with the weighted convergence theorem from Section 4 to prove the sharp dimension estimate in the the case β>0\beta>0. As discussed above, each gg-harmonic function hh can be properly blown-down to a limit which is a harmonic function on 𝒞a\mathcal{C}_{a}. To get a dimension estimate, one still needs to ensure that this process is injective from ℋd​(g)\mathcal{H}_{d}(g) to ℋd​(𝒞a)\mathcal{H}_{d}(\mathcal{C}_{a}). The standard L2L^{2} inner product can be used on balls of fixed radius to maintain linear independence. Therefore it is desirable to find a common sequence of radius Rq=2q​R0→∞R_{q}=2^{q}R_{0}\to\infty (see Corollary 5.7), along which gg-harmonic functions are simultaneously blown-down. This technique is inspired by Lin’s argument for asymptotically conic elliptic operators [25, Theorem 2.13]. Moreover, this technique also helps to establish the surjectivity of blow-down process, thus leading to a precise value of ℋd​(g)\mathcal{H}_{d}(g).

Let g=e2​w​g0g=e^{2w}g_{0} be a complete conformal metric on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, n≥3n\geq 3, satisfying Ricg≥0\operatorname{Ric}_{g}\geq 0, and suppose that its asymptotic volume ratio β\beta is positive. Then the asymptotic exponent of the conformal factor is m∈[0,1)m\in[0,1), and we set a:=1−m.a:=1-m.

By the exact volume-ratio formula recalled in the introduction 1.2,

β=an−1.\beta=a^{n-1}.

If m=0m=0, then β=1\beta=1; the equality case in the Bishop–Gromov volume comparison implies that (ℝn,g)(\mathbb{R}^{n},g) is isometric to Euclidean space. Thus the only case in which a strict dimension drop can occur is

0<m<1,0<a<1,0<m<1,\qquad 0<a<1,

which we assume througout the section.

For any real number d≥0d\geq 0, recall

ℋd(g):={h:Δgh=0,|h(x)|≤Ch(1+dg(0,x)d)}.\mathcal{H}_{d}(g):=\left\{h:\Delta_{g}h=0,\quad|h(x)|\leq C_{h}\bigl(1+d_{g}(0,x)^{d}\bigr)\right\}.

For a nonzero gg-harmonic function hh, define its normalized weighted L2L^{2} mass on the Euclidean ball BR⊂ℝnB_{R}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} by

(5.1) Sh​(R):=∫BRh2​⁡d​μgμg​(BR),S_{h}(R):=\frac{\displaystyle\int_{B_{R}}h^{2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu_{g}}{\displaystyle\mu_{g}(B_{R})},

where d​μg:=en​w​(x)​⁡d​xd\mu_{g}:=e^{nw(x)}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x is the volume measure of (ℝn,g)(\mathbb{R}^{n},g). This captures the L2L^{2} growth rate of hh on Euclidean balls.

5.3. Simultaneous blow-down and the dimension estimate


We can now complete the proof of Theorem C. We divide into two parts: Theorem 5.8 and Theorem 5.10.

Theorem 5.8.

Let g=e2​w​g0g=e^{2w}g_{0} be a complete non-flat conformal metric on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, n≥3n\geq 3, satisfying Ricg≥0\operatorname{Ric}_{g}\geq 0 and β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1). Then, for any positive number d>0d>0,

(5.18) dimℋd​(g)≤dimℋd​(𝒞a)=dimℋd¯−1​(g0)≤{dimℋd−1​(g0),if ​d∈ℤ,dimℋd​(g0),if ​d∉ℤ,\dim\mathcal{H}_{d}(g)\leq\dim\mathcal{H}_{d}(\mathcal{C}_{a})=\dim\mathcal{H}_{\bar{d}-1}(g_{0})\leq\begin{cases}\dim\mathcal{H}_{d-1}(g_{0}),&\text{if }d\in\mathbb{Z},\\ \dim\mathcal{H}_{d}(g_{0}),&\text{if }d\not\in\mathbb{Z},\end{cases}

6. Completion of the proof of TheoremA

We now pass from the globally conformal case treated in the preceding sections to an arbitrary complete locally conformally flat manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature. The remaining cases are elementary. We recall that the classification theorems of Zhu [33, Theorem 1] and of Carron–Herzlich [4, Theorem A] imply that a connected complete locally conformally flat manifold (Mn,g)(M^{n},g), n≥3n\geq 3, with Ricg≥0\operatorname{Ric}_{g}\geq 0 belongs to one of the following classes:

  1. (1)

    MM is non-flat and globally conformally equivalent to ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n};

  2. (2)

    MM is globally conformally equivalent to a spherical space form;

  3. (3)

    MM is locally isometric to the round cylinder ℝ×𝕊n−1\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{S}^{n-1};

  4. (4)

    MM is a complete flat manifold.

We shall discuss case by case and thereby complete the proof of Theorem A. For reader’s convenience and simplicity, we recall it here with a statement only for integer growth rate dd. We refer the reader to the Remark  6.2 below for non-integer growth rate.

Theorem 6.1.

Let (Mn,g)(M^{n},g), n≥3n\geq 3, be a connected complete locally conformally flat manifold satisfying Ricg≥0\operatorname{Ric}_{g}\geq 0. Then, for every integer d≥0d\geq 0,

(6.1) hd​(M)≤hd​(ℝn).h_{d}(M)\leq h_{d}(\mathbb{R}^{n}).

Moreover, if equality holds for some integer d≥1d\geq 1, then (M,g)(M,g) is isometric to the Euclidean space.

Remark 6.2.

By Theorem 5.8, it is easy to see that 6.1 also holds for non-integer dd.

However, one cannot expect the rigidity. In fact, by Theorem 5.10, for every d∈(1,2)d\in(1,2), there exists a∈(0,1)a\in(0,1) such that d¯=2\bar{d}=2, so that the corresponding conformal metric gg on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} is non-flat and satisfies

Ricg≥0,βg>0,\operatorname{Ric}_{g}\geq 0,\qquad\beta_{g}>0,

and

dimℋd​(ℝn,g)=dimℋd​(𝒞a)=dimℋd¯−1​(ℝn,g0)=n+1.\dim\mathcal{H}_{d}(\mathbb{R}^{n},g)=\dim\mathcal{H}_{d}(\mathcal{C}_{a})=\dim\mathcal{H}_{\bar{d}-1}(\mathbb{R}^{n},g_{0})=n+1.

6.1. The globally conformal non-flat case


Suppose first that MM belongs to class (1). Thus

(Mn,g)≅(ℝn,e2​w​g0)(M^{n},g)\cong(\mathbb{R}^{n},e^{2w}g_{0})

with gg non-flat. Let β\beta denote its asymptotic volume ratio.

If β=0\beta=0, Theorem B gives

ℋd​(M)=ℝ\mathcal{H}_{d}(M)=\mathbb{R}

for every finite dd. Hence

hd​(M)=1≤hd​(ℝn),∀d≥0,h_{d}(M)=1\leq h_{d}(\mathbb{R}^{n}),\quad\forall d\geq 0,

and the inequality is strict whenever d≥1d\geq 1.

If β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1), Theorem C gives, for every integer d≥1d\geq 1,

hd​(M)≤hd−1​(ℝn)<hd​(ℝn).h_{d}(M)\leq h_{d-1}(\mathbb{R}^{n})<h_{d}(\mathbb{R}^{n}).

For d=0d=0, both spaces consist of constants. Thus the theorem holds in this class, and equality for a positive degree is impossible.

6.2. The spherical case


Suppose that MM belongs to class (2). A spherical space form is compact, and global conformal equivalence preserves compactness. Hence MM is compact. Every harmonic function on a connected compact manifold is constant, so

ℋd​(M)=ℝfor every ​d≥0.\mathcal{H}_{d}(M)=\mathbb{R}\qquad\text{for every }d\geq 0.

Consequently,

hd​(M)=1≤hd​(ℝn),h_{d}(M)=1\leq h_{d}(\mathbb{R}^{n}),

with strict inequality for every d≥1d\geq 1.

For the remaining two cases, the universal cover of MM is either isometric to the standard cylinder C=ℝ×𝕊n−1C=\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{S}^{n-1} or the standard ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, where one has clear understanding of ℋd​(M~)\mathcal{H}_{d}(\widetilde{M}). The lift of a harmonic function on MM to M~\widetilde{M} preserves the polynomial growth rate and is deck transformation group invariant. Using these facts, one also has an explicit description for ℋd​(M)\mathcal{H}_{d}(M).

6.3. The cylindrical case


We first classify polynomial-growth harmonic functions on the standard cylinder ℝ×𝕊n−1\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{S}^{n-1}.

Lemma 6.3.

Let CC be the standard cylinder with the product metric d​t2+g𝕊n−1dt^{2}+g_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}, then every harmonic function on CC having polynomial growth is of the form

(6.2) u⁡(t,θ)=A+B​t.u(t,\theta)=A+Bt.

In particular,

dimℋd​(C)={1,0≤d<1,2,d≥1.\dim\mathcal{H}_{d}(C)=\begin{cases}1,&0\leq d<1,\\ 2,&d\geq 1.\end{cases}
Proof.

Let {Yℓ,α}\{Y_{\ell,\alpha}\} be an orthonormal basis of spherical harmonics satisfying

−Δ𝕊n−1​Yℓ,α=λℓ​Yℓ,α,λℓ=ℓ⁡(ℓ+n−2).-\Delta_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}Y_{\ell,\alpha}=\lambda_{\ell}Y_{\ell,\alpha},\qquad\lambda_{\ell}=\ell(\ell+n-2).

For a harmonic function uu on CC, set

aℓ,α​(t):=∫𝕊n−1u⁡(t,θ)​Yℓ,α​(θ)​𝑑θ.a_{\ell,\alpha}(t):=\int_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}u(t,\theta)Y_{\ell,\alpha}(\theta)\,d\theta.

Since

ΔC=∂t2+Δ𝕊n−1,\Delta_{C}=\partial_{t}^{2}+\Delta_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}},

each coefficient satisfies

(6.3) aℓ,α′′−λℓ​aℓ,α=0.a_{\ell,\alpha}^{\prime\prime}-\lambda_{\ell}a_{\ell,\alpha}=0.

The polynomial-growth assumption on uu implies the same polynomial bound for every coefficient aℓ,αa_{\ell,\alpha} as t→±∞t\to\pm\infty.

For ℓ=0\ell=0, equation 6.3 gives

a0′′=0,a_{0}^{\prime\prime}=0,

so a0​(t)=A+B​ta_{0}(t)=A+Bt. If ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1, then

aℓ,α​(t)=cℓ,α+​eλℓ​t+cℓ,α−​e−λℓ​t.a_{\ell,\alpha}(t)=c_{\ell,\alpha}^{+}e^{\sqrt{\lambda_{\ell}}t}+c_{\ell,\alpha}^{-}e^{-\sqrt{\lambda_{\ell}}t}.

Polynomial growth as t→+∞t\to+\infty forces cℓ,α+=0c_{\ell,\alpha}^{+}=0, while polynomial growth as t→−∞t\to-\infty forces cℓ,α−=0c_{\ell,\alpha}^{-}=0. Thus every positive spherical mode vanishes, and 6.2 follows. The final dimension assertion is immediate. ∎

We then exploit the structure of the deck transformation group to determine ℋd​(M)\mathcal{H}_{d}(M) precisely. If MM is compact, the computation is trivial, so we mainly focus in the case that MM is complete noncompact.

Let MM be a complete noncompact manifold locally isometric to CC. Since n≥3n\geq 3, CC is simply connected and is therefore the Riemannian universal cover of MM. Thus

M=C/Γ,M=C/\Gamma,

where Γ⊂Isom⁡(C)\Gamma\subset\operatorname{Isom}(C) is a discrete group acting freely and properly discontinuously on CC.

Note the product decomposition of CC is preserved by every isometry. Hence

Isom⁡(C)=Isom⁡(ℝ)×O⁡(n),\operatorname{Isom}(C)=\operatorname{Isom}(\mathbb{R})\times O(n),

and every γ∈Γ\gamma\in\Gamma has the form

γ⁡(t,θ)=(εγ​t+aγ,Aγ​θ),\gamma(t,\theta)=\bigl(\varepsilon_{\gamma}t+a_{\gamma},A_{\gamma}\theta\bigr),

where εγ∈{±1},aγ∈ℝ, and ​Aγ∈O⁡(n)\varepsilon_{\gamma}\in\{\pm 1\},a_{\gamma}\in\mathbb{R},\text{ and }A_{\gamma}\in O(n).

Consider the natural projection

p:Γ⟶Isom⁡(ℝ),p⁡(γ)​(t)=εγ​t+aγ.p:\Gamma\longrightarrow\operatorname{Isom}(\mathbb{R}),\qquad p(\gamma)(t)=\varepsilon_{\gamma}t+a_{\gamma}.
Proposition 6.4.

Let MnM^{n}, n≥3n\geq 3, be a complete noncompact manifold locally isometric to the round cylinder ℝ×𝕊n−1\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{S}^{n-1}. Then the image p⁡(Γ)p(\Gamma) is either trivial or a group of order two generated by a reflection of ℝ\mathbb{R}. Moreover,

hd​(M)={1,0≤d<1,2,d≥1​and ​p​(Γ)={e},1,d≥1​and ​p​(Γ)≠{e}.h_{d}(M)=\begin{cases}1,&0\leq d<1,\\[2.84526pt] 2,&d\geq 1\ \text{and }p(\Gamma)=\{e\},\\[2.84526pt] 1,&d\geq 1\ \text{and }p(\Gamma)\neq\{e\}.\end{cases}
Proof.

We first describe the possible image of the deck transformation group on the ℝ\mathbb{R}-factor. The subgroup p⁡(Γ)p(\Gamma) is discrete in Isom⁡(ℝ)\operatorname{Isom}(\mathbb{R}). Indeed, if there were a sequence of distinct elements γj∈Γ\gamma_{j}\in\Gamma such that p⁡(γj)p(\gamma_{j}) converged in Isom⁡(ℝ)\operatorname{Isom}(\mathbb{R}), then, since O⁡(n)O(n) is compact, a subsequence of AγjA_{\gamma_{j}} would also converge. It would follow that γj​γk−1\gamma_{j}\gamma_{k}^{-1} can be made arbitrarily close to the identity for large j,kj,k, contradicting the discreteness of Γ\Gamma.

Similarly, F:=ker⁡pF:=\ker p is finite, since it is a discrete subgroup of the compact group O⁡(n)O(n). Note that the discrete subgroups of Isom⁡(ℝ)\operatorname{Isom}(\mathbb{R}) are, up to conjugation,

{e},ℤ2,ℤ,D∞,\{e\},\qquad\mathbb{Z}_{2},\qquad\mathbb{Z},\qquad D_{\infty},

where ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} is generated by a reflection and D∞D_{\infty} is the infinite dihedral group. Since the last two groups act cocompactly on ℝ\mathbb{R}, and 𝕊n−1\mathbb{S}^{n-1} is compact, if p⁡(Γ)p(\Gamma) contains a nontrivial translation, then C/ΓC/\Gamma would be compact. Then the noncompactness of MM implies

p⁡(Γ)={e}orp⁡(Γ)≅ℤ2.p(\Gamma)=\{e\}\qquad\text{or}\qquad p(\Gamma)\cong\mathbb{Z}_{2}.

If p⁡(Γ)={e}p(\Gamma)=\{e\}, then every deck transformation acts only on the sphere:

γ⁡(t,θ)=(t,Aγ​θ).\gamma(t,\theta)=(t,A_{\gamma}\theta).

Thus

M≅ℝ×(𝕊n−1/F),M\cong\mathbb{R}\times\bigl(\mathbb{S}^{n-1}/F\bigr),

where F⊂O⁡(n)F\subset O(n) is a finite group acting freely on 𝕊n−1\mathbb{S}^{n-1}.

If p⁡(Γ)≅ℤ2p(\Gamma)\cong\mathbb{Z}_{2}, then Γ\Gamma contains an element γ0\gamma_{0} whose action on the ℝ\mathbb{R}-factor is a reflection, which has the form

γ0​(t,θ)=(−t+a,A​θ)\gamma_{0}(t,\theta)=(-t+a,A\theta)

for some A∈O⁡(n)A\in O(n).

We now turn to polynomial growth harmonic functions. Let u∈ℋd​(M)u\in\mathcal{H}_{d}(M) and let

u~:=u∘π\widetilde{u}:=u\circ\pi

be its lift to CC. For fixed base points p~∈C\widetilde{p}\in C and p=π⁡(p~)p=\pi(\widetilde{p}), notice

dM​(p,π⁡(x~))≤dC​(p~,x~),d_{M}\bigl(p,\pi(\widetilde{x})\bigr)\leq d_{C}(\widetilde{p},\widetilde{x}),

so u~\widetilde{u} has polynomial growth of degree at most dd on CC. By Lemma 6.3, we have

(6.4) u~​(t,θ)=A+B​t.\widetilde{u}(t,\theta)=A+Bt.

Since u~\widetilde{u} is the lift of uu via the universal covering, it must satisfy

u~∘γ=u~for every ​γ∈Γ.\widetilde{u}\circ\gamma=\widetilde{u}\qquad\text{for every }\gamma\in\Gamma.

If p⁡(Γ)={e}p(\Gamma)=\{e\}, the function tt itself is Γ\Gamma-invariant and hence descends to MM. Consequently,

ℋd​(M)={ℝ,0≤d<1,span⁡{1,t},d≥1,\mathcal{H}_{d}(M)=\begin{cases}\mathbb{R},&0\leq d<1,\\[2.84526pt] \operatorname{span}\{1,t\},&d\geq 1,\end{cases}

where, by abuse of notation, tt denotes the descended function on MM.

If p⁡(Γ)≅ℤ2p(\Gamma)\cong\mathbb{Z}_{2}, consider a reflection element of Γ\Gamma

γ0​(t,θ)=(−t+a,A​θ).\gamma_{0}(t,\theta)=(-t+a,A\theta).

The invariance of 6.4 under γ0\gamma_{0} gives B=0.B=0. Hence every polynomial-growth harmonic function on MM is constant. Then the formula for hd​(M)h_{d}(M) is immediate. ∎

6.4. The flat case


Finally we consider the class (4). Let MnM^{n} be a connected complete flat manifold. then its universal cover is ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. By the Cheeger-Gromoll soul theorem, MM admits a compact totally geodesic flat soul Σk\Sigma^{k}. Since the inclusion Σ↪M\Sigma\hookrightarrow M is a homotopy equivalence, it induces an isomorphism on fundamental groups. Then the inverse image of Σ\Sigma in the universal cover ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} is connected and is therefore an affine subspace V≅ℝkV\cong\mathbb{R}^{k}. The group of deck transformation Γ=π1​(M)\Gamma=\pi_{1}(M) preserves VV and acts cocompactly on it. By virtue of the Bieberbach theorem, after identifying

ℝn=V⊕V⟂,\mathbb{R}^{n}=V\oplus V^{\perp},

each γ∈Γ\gamma\in\Gamma takes the form

γ⁡(x,y)=(Aγ​x+aγ,Bγ​y),Aγ∈O⁡(k),aγ∈ℝk,Bγ∈O⁡(n−k).\gamma(x,y)=\bigl(A_{\gamma}x+a_{\gamma},B_{\gamma}y\bigr),\qquad A_{\gamma}\in O(k),\quad a_{\gamma}\in\mathbb{R}^{k},\quad B_{\gamma}\in O(n-k).

Consequently, MM is the total space of a flat Riemannian vector bundle over the compact flat manifold Σk=V/Γ\Sigma^{k}=V/\Gamma.

Let

K:={Bγ:γ∈Γ}¯⊂O(n−k)K:=\overline{\{B_{\gamma}:\gamma\in\Gamma\}}\subset O(n-k)

be the closure of the normal holonomy group. For ℓ≥0\ell\geq 0, denote by 𝒴ℓ​(ℝn−k)\mathcal{Y}_{\ell}(\mathbb{R}^{n-k}) the space of homogeneous harmonic polynomials of degree ℓ\ell on ℝn−k\mathbb{R}^{n-k}.

Proposition 6.5.

Let MnM^{n} be a connected complete flat manifold and let the notation be as above. For every real number d≥0d\geq 0, putting D=⌊d⌋D=\lfloor d\rfloor, there is a natural isomorphism

ℋd​(M)≅⨁ℓ=0D𝒴ℓ​(ℝn−k)K,\mathcal{H}_{d}(M)\cong\bigoplus_{\ell=0}^{D}\mathcal{Y}_{\ell}(\mathbb{R}^{n-k})^{K},

where the superscript KK denotes the KK-invariant subspace. Consequently,

hd​(M)=∑ℓ=0Ddim𝒴ℓ​(ℝn−k)K≤hd​(ℝn−k)≤hd​(ℝn).h_{d}(M)=\sum_{\ell=0}^{D}\dim\mathcal{Y}_{\ell}(\mathbb{R}^{n-k})^{K}\leq h_{d}(\mathbb{R}^{n-k})\leq h_{d}(\mathbb{R}^{n}).

In particular, if hd​(M)=hd​(ℝn)h_{d}(M)=h_{d}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) for some real number d≥1d\geq 1, then MnM^{n} is isometric to ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}.

Proof.

Let π:ℝn⟶M\pi:\mathbb{R}^{n}\longrightarrow M be the universal covering map and let u∈ℋd​(M)u\in\mathcal{H}_{d}(M). Then its lift u~:=u∘π\widetilde{u}:=u\circ\pi is harmonic on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. As discussed in Proposition  6.4 above, the lift u~\widetilde{u} has polynomial growth of degree at most dd, and

u~∘γ=u~for every ​γ∈Γ.\widetilde{u}\circ\gamma=\widetilde{u}\qquad\text{for every }\gamma\in\Gamma.

We claim that u~\widetilde{u} is independent of the VV-variable. Indeed, since Σ=V/Γ\Sigma=V/\Gamma is a compact flat manifold, Bieberbach’s theorem provides a finite-index subgroup Λ⊂Γ\Lambda\subset\Gamma whose induced action on VV consists of translations by a full lattice in VV. Thus, for λ∈Λ\lambda\in\Lambda,

λ⁡(x,y)=(x+aλ,Bλ​y),\lambda(x,y)=(x+a_{\lambda},B_{\lambda}y),

where Bλ∈O⁡(n−k)B_{\lambda}\in O(n-k) and the vectors aλa_{\lambda} span VV.

Fix such a λ∈Λ\lambda\in\Lambda. The Γ\Gamma-invariance of u~\widetilde{u} gives

u~​(x+j​aλ,Bλj​y)=u~​(x,y),∀j∈ℤ.\widetilde{u}(x+ja_{\lambda},B_{\lambda}^{j}y)=\widetilde{u}(x,y),\qquad\forall j\in\mathbb{Z}.

Since Bλ∈O⁡(n−k)B_{\lambda}\in O(n-k), there exists a sequence ji→∞j_{i}\to\infty such that Bλji⟶I.B_{\lambda}^{j_{i}}\longrightarrow I. Suppose for contradiction that u~\widetilde{u} had positive polynomial degree in the aλa_{\lambda}-direction, then, after dividing the preceding identity by the highest corresponding power of jij_{i} and letting i→∞i\to\infty, its leading coefficient in that direction would have to vanish. This implies

∂aλu~=0,∀aλ∈V,\partial_{a_{\lambda}}\widetilde{u}=0,\quad\forall a_{\lambda}\in V,

from which we conclude that

u~​(x,y)=P​(y)\widetilde{u}(x,y)=P(y)

for some harmonic polynomial PP on V⟂≅ℝn−kV^{\perp}\cong\mathbb{R}^{n-k}. Furthermore, the Γ\Gamma-invariance of u~\tilde{u} becomes

P⁡(Bγ​y)=P⁡(y),γ∈Γ.P(B_{\gamma}y)=P(y),\qquad\gamma\in\Gamma.

By continuity this is equivalent to

P⁡(B​y)=P⁡(y),∀B∈K.P(By)=P(y),\qquad\forall B\in K.

Thus PP is a KK-invariant harmonic polynomial on ℝn−k\mathbb{R}^{n-k}.

Conversely, every KK-invariant harmonic polynomial PP on ℝn−k\mathbb{R}^{n-k}, regarded as a function on V⊕V⟂V\oplus V^{\perp} by

(x,y)⟼P⁡(y),(x,y)\longmapsto P(y),

is Γ\Gamma-invariant and hence descends to a harmonic function on MM. Its polynomial degree agrees with its growth degree on MM. Indeed, if Σ⊂M\Sigma\subset M denotes the soul, then

dM​(π⁡(x,y),Σ)=|y|,d_{M}(\pi(x,y),\Sigma)=|y|,

while, for a fixed p∈Σp\in\Sigma,

|y|≤dM​(π⁡(x,y),p)≤|y|+diam⁡(Σ).|y|\leq d_{M}(\pi(x,y),p)\leq|y|+\operatorname{diam}(\Sigma).

It follows that

ℋd​(M)≅⨁ℓ=0D𝒴ℓ​(ℝn−k)K.\mathcal{H}_{d}(M)\cong\bigoplus_{\ell=0}^{D}\mathcal{Y}_{\ell}(\mathbb{R}^{n-k})^{K}.

Taking dimensions gives

hd​(M)=∑ℓ=0Ddim𝒴ℓ​(ℝn−k)K≤∑ℓ=0Ddim𝒴ℓ​(ℝn−k)=hd​(ℝn−k)≤hd​(ℝn).h_{d}(M)=\sum_{\ell=0}^{D}\dim\mathcal{Y}_{\ell}(\mathbb{R}^{n-k})^{K}\leq\sum_{\ell=0}^{D}\dim\mathcal{Y}_{\ell}(\mathbb{R}^{n-k})=h_{d}(\mathbb{R}^{n-k})\leq h_{d}(\mathbb{R}^{n}).

Finally, suppose that the equality hd​(M)=hd​(ℝn)h_{d}(M)=h_{d}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) holds for some real number d≥1d\geq 1. Then the above inequalities imply n−k=nn-k=n, K={e}K=\{e\} and M≅ℝnM\cong\mathbb{R}^{n} isometrically. ∎
